title: Four steps per exam problem (with minutes)
ask: What are the four steps for each 22-minute problem, and how many minutes go to each?
items: Read and mark (3 minutes): who acted, under what power, exact words, numbers, dates, the question asked.
Spot and outline (3 minutes): run the issue checklist; pick 2–3 decisive issues, one anchor case each.
Write (14 minutes): about 150–180 words; answer first, then rule, application, conclusion.
Check (2 minutes): did I answer the question actually asked, and cite a provision and a case?
src: Exam method (rule map 00); 1 hr 30 min, four problems, one yellow sheet

title: The ALAC template
ask: What do the four letters of ALAC stand for, in order?
items: A – Answer: lead with Yes/No or ‘Section 4 is unconstitutional.’
L – Law: the provision and an anchor case.
A – Application: tie the rule to the exact words of the law or the facts.
C – Conclusion: one sentence that answers again.
src: Exam method (rule map 00); Gatmaytan block intel

title: Gatmaytan’s four question shapes
ask: What are the four question shapes Gatmaytan uses on exams?
items: ‘Determine the constitutionality of Section X of RA ___’ (text quoted; the defect hides in one phrase).
‘Resolve the legal issues in this story’ or ‘critique this official’s statement’ (find every issue).
‘How does the new law address the issues in [case]?’ (state the case’s issue, show the statute’s fix).
‘Assume X challenges this; resolve it in his favor’ (argue one side; do not hedge).
src: Exam method (rule map 00): 2020 quizzes; 2023 Q1, Q3; 2024 Q2–Q4

title: Order of the procedural paragraph
ask: In what order do you write the two- or three-line procedural paragraph before the merits?
items: Remedy and forum (Rule 65 in the SC, declaratory relief in the RTC, tribunal, COA).
Actual case and ripeness: is it only a bill, a proposal, a draft IRR?
Standing: who is suing, and in what capacity?
Mootness: have events overtaken the case (and does an exception apply)?
src: Exam method and JR rule map (‘In a news question’ box)
hook: Forum → Ripe → Party → Moot, then merits

title: The eight-heading issue checklist
ask: What are the eight headings of the margin issue checklist?
items: Court and procedure (actual case, ripeness/mootness, standing, earliest opportunity, lis mota, remedy, forum).
Who acted and under what power (Congress, one House, committee, President, agency, LGU, private party).
Separation of powers (encroachment, legislative veto, Congress interpreting the Constitution).
Delegation (completeness and sufficient-standard tests, IRR requisites, publication, subdelegation).
How the law was made (title/one subject, origination, riders, savings, tax exemptions).
Congress internally (officers, quorum, rules, discipline, privileges, offices, tribunals, CA).
Inherent powers (police power, eminent domain, non-impairment, state immunity).
People (citizenship, election of citizenship, RA 9225, residence, suffrage).
src: Exam method (rule map 00), issue checklist

title: Tribe’s six modes of constitutional argument
ask: What are Tribe’s six modes of constitutional interpretation (Gatmaytan, Legal Method Essentials)?
items: Textualism: the words alone, read in linguistic context.
Structural analysis: what the arrangement of the text implies (e.g., separation of powers).
Originalism: what the framers consciously intended.
Normative or pragmatic approach: the nation’s ethos, moral and political identity.
Judicial precedent (stare decisis): decisional doctrine; gives flexibility and stability.
Combination of the above.
src: Tribe, in Gatmaytan, Legal Method Essentials (Ch. 1–3); class reviewer
hook: T-S-O-N-P-C: Text, Structure, Origin, Norms, Precedent, Combo

title: Weak points of the Tribe modes
ask: What is the main weakness (or advantage) of each of these modes: textualism, originalism, normative argument, precedent?
items: Textualism: words are ambiguous or self-contradictory, and it risks freezing the Constitution into obsolescence.
Originalism: framers, drafters and ratifiers did not share a single purpose.
Originalism: historical records are often inconclusive and contradictory.
Originalism: subordinates ratified text to subjective, un-enacted intentions; abstract intentions over concrete expectations.
Normative/pragmatic: inappropriate subjectivity; appeals to values not properly part of constitutional law.
Precedent (advantages): flexibility to adapt over time, and stability because judges must follow it.
src: Tribe, in Gatmaytan, Legal Method Essentials; class reviewer

title: The three classic aids to construction
ask: What are the three classic principles of constitutional construction (as listed in Francisco), with their anchor cases?
items: Verba legis: words take their ordinary meaning unless technical terms are used (J.M. Tuason).
Ratio legis est anima: if unclear, follow the intent of the framers and the ratifying people (Nitafan; Civil Liberties Union).
Ut magis valeat quam pereat: read as a whole; harmonize so every word is operative (Civil Liberties Union).
src: Francisco v. House (2003); J.M. Tuason; Nitafan; Civil Liberties Union v. Exec. Sec.

title: Other interpretive rules (class reviewer)
ask: Besides the three classic canons, what other rules of constitutional interpretation are in the materials?
items: Prospectivity: provisions apply prospectively unless they say otherwise (Filoteo).
Expressio unius est exclusio alterius: express mention of some of a class excludes others.
Provisions are generally mandatory, not directory.
Presumption of self-execution (Manila Prince Hotel).
No mandate is given primacy over another unless the Constitution makes its primacy clear (Kida v. Senate).
Literal meaning yields only where it would be impossible, absurd or unjust (Vicencio v. Villar).
Interpretation belongs to the courts; Congress cannot declare a provision’s meaning by statute (Endencia).
src: Class reviewer (Principles of Constitutional Construction); Filoteo; Manila Prince; Endencia

title: When a constitutional provision is merely directory
ask: Constitutional provisions are generally mandatory. What three conditions make a provision directory instead?
items: No consequential rights or liabilities depend on it.
No injury can result from ignoring it.
Its purpose can be accomplished in a manner other than that prescribed.
src: Class reviewer (Mandatory and directory provisions)

title: Test for a self-executing provision
ask: Under Manila Prince Hotel, when is a constitutional provision self-executing? (four elements)
items: It is complete in itself and operative without enabling legislation.
The nature and extent of the right conferred are fixed by the Constitution.
The liability imposed is fixed by the Constitution.
Nothing indicates the subject is referred to Congress for action.
src: Manila Prince Hotel v. GSIS (1997)

title: Self-execution: rule, exception, exception to the exception
ask: State the general rule on self-execution, its exception, the exceptions to that exception, and the reason for the presumption.
items: General rule: provisions are presumed self-executing unless they expressly require legislation.
Reason: a contrary presumption would let Congress nullify the Constitution by not legislating.
Exception: Art. II principles and policies are not self-executing; they guide courts and Congress.
Exception to exception: Art. II, Secs. 15–16 (health; balanced and healthful ecology), per Oposa v. Factoran.
2026: Kapatiran treats Art. II, Sec. 26 (political dynasties) as a mandatory duty enforceable by mandamus.
src: Manila Prince Hotel; Oposa v. Factoran; Kapatiran Party v. Congress (2026)

title: Kapatiran’s three questions on a ‘shall … as defined by law’ clause
ask: After Kapatiran (2026), what three questions do you keep apart when a provision says the State ‘shall’ act ‘as may be defined by law’?
items: Does the provision impose a duty (‘shall’)?
Who defines its content (‘as may be defined by law’ means Congress)?
Can courts enforce it (grave abuse by inaction under Art. VIII, Sec. 1; mandamus)?
src: Kapatiran Party v. Congress (Aug. 26, 2026); Art. II, Sec. 26

title: The judges’ salary line of cases
ask: Trace the three cases on taxing judges’ salaries, in order, with each holding.
items: Perfecto v. Meer (1950): income tax on a judge’s salary is a prohibited diminution (1935 Constitution).
Endencia v. David (1953): RA 590 declaring such tax ‘not a diminution’ is void; Congress cannot interpret the Constitution.
Nitafan v. CIR (1987): under the 1987 Constitution framers intended salaries taxable; Perfecto and Endencia discarded.
src: Perfecto; Endencia; Nitafan

title: When Congress may fix another salary rate for judges
ask: Under Nitafan, on what two conditions may Congress fix a different salary rate for Justices and judges?
items: The new rate is higher than what they receive when the law is enacted; or
If lower, it applies only to those appointed after the law’s enactment.
src: Nitafan v. CIR (1987); Art. VIII, Sec. 10 (salary ‘shall not be decreased’ during continuance in office)

title: Three modes of proposing changes (Art. XVII)
ask: What are the three modes of proposing amendments or revisions, with the vote or signatures each needs?
items: Congress as constituent assembly: ‘a vote of three-fourths of all its Members’ (Sec. 1(1)); amendment or revision.
Constitutional convention (Sec. 1(2)); amendment or revision.
People’s initiative: petition of at least 12% of all registered voters, at least 3% in every district (Sec. 2); amendments only.
src: Art. XVII, Secs. 1–2

title: Two ways Congress calls a constitutional convention
ask: Under Art. XVII, Sec. 3, what are the two ways Congress may bring about a constitutional convention, and the vote for each?
items: Call the convention directly ‘by a vote of two-thirds of all its Members’.
‘By a majority vote of all its Members, submit to the electorate the question of calling such a convention.’
src: Art. XVII, Sec. 3

title: Requirements and limits of a people’s initiative (Art. XVII, Sec. 2)
ask: What does Art. XVII, Sec. 2 require of, and how does it limit, a people’s initiative on the Constitution?
items: Amendments only, never revisions.
Petition of ‘at least twelve per centum of the total number of registered voters’.
Every legislative district represented by ‘at least three per centum of the registered voters therein’.
Not ‘within five years following the ratification of this Constitution’.
Not ‘oftener than once every five years thereafter’.
‘The Congress shall provide for the implementation’: needs an enabling law (not self-executing, Santiago).
src: Art. XVII, Sec. 2; Santiago v. COMELEC (1997); Lambino (2006)

title: Ratification of amendments and revisions (Art. XVII, Sec. 4)
ask: What are the requirements for ratifying an amendment or revision, and from when is the plebiscite period counted?
items: Ratified ‘by a majority of the votes cast in a plebiscite’.
Plebiscite ‘not earlier than sixty days nor later than ninety days’ after the trigger date.
Congress or convention proposals (Sec. 1): counted from ‘the approval of such amendment or revision’.
Initiative (Sec. 2): counted from ‘the certification by the Commission on Elections of the sufficiency of the petition’.
src: Art. XVII, Sec. 4

title: Amendment versus revision: contrasts
ask: Give the contrasts between an amendment and a revision (Lambino; class reviewer table).
items: Amendment adds, reduces or deletes without altering basic principles; revision alters a basic principle (separation of powers, checks and balances).
Amendment affects only the specific provision amended; revision affects several provisions or the substantial entirety.
Amendment improves or better carries out the original purpose, within the lines of the original constitution.
Amendment: any of the three modes; revision: constituent assembly or convention only, never initiative.
src: Lambino v. COMELEC (2006); class reviewer

title: Lambino’s two-part test: amendment or revision?
ask: What two tests does Lambino use to tell a revision from an amendment?
items: Quantitative: is the change so extensive that it alters the substantial entirety of the Constitution?
Qualitative: does it make far-reaching changes to the basic plan of government (e.g., presidential to parliamentary, bicameral to unicameral)?
src: Lambino v. COMELEC (2006)
hook: How MUCH changes vs. WHAT KIND changes; either = revision

title: Lambino’s requisites of an initiative petition
ask: What must an initiative petition satisfy under Lambino to be ‘directly proposed by the people … upon a petition’?
items: The people must author, and so personally sign, the entire proposal.
The proposal must be embodied in a petition.
The full text is on the face of the petition or attached to it.
If attached, the petition must say so.
The full text must be shown to the people before they sign (a signature sheet is not the petition).
src: Lambino v. COMELEC (2006); Art. XVII, Sec. 2

title: Why the Lambino initiative failed
ask: On what grounds was the Lambino initiative dismissed (8–7)?
items: The signature sheets did not contain the text of the proposal; the sheet is not the ‘petition’.
Quantitatively a revision: it overhauled Arts. VI and VII, affecting 105 provisions.
Qualitatively a revision: presidential to parliamentary, bicameral to unicameral.
No need to revisit Santiago (RA 6735 inadequate), since the petition already failed.
COMELEC committed no grave abuse in following Santiago.
src: Lambino v. COMELEC (2006); Gatmaytan, ‘Changing Constitutions’

title: Why RA 6735 is inadequate for constitutional initiatives
ask: Why did Santiago v. COMELEC hold RA 6735 inadequate for initiatives on the Constitution?
items: Sec. 2 of the Act (statement of policy) is silent on amendments to the Constitution; ‘Constitution’ there is an afterthought.
Unlike other initiatives, the Act does not provide the contents of a petition on the Constitution.
No subtitle on constitutional initiative (only national and local initiative subtitles).
No procedures for gathering and verifying signatures or determining sufficiency.
COMELEC cannot fill the gap by resolution: Res. No. 2300 void (undue delegation, ultra vires).
src: Santiago v. COMELEC (1997); Gatmaytan’s book (three reasons); class reviewer

title: Doctrine of proper submission
ask: What are the rules under the doctrine of proper submission?
items: A plebiscite may coincide with a general election, if the people can still be informed (Gonzales).
All proposals of one convention go to the people together at one plebiscite (Tolentino).
The people must have a full ‘frame of reference’ (Tolentino).
No piecemeal submission, e.g., a voting-age amendment ahead of the rest (Tolentino).
src: Gonzales v. COMELEC (1967); Tolentino v. COMELEC (1971)

title: Joint or separate voting in a constituent assembly
ask: The three-fourths vote is unclear on joint or separate voting. What are the points for separate voting (V. V. Mendoza’s solution)?
items: The text is silent; the question is open (say so, and note the contrary joint-vote reading).
Convene in joint session but vote separately, as under the 1935 Constitution.
Bicameral structure of Art. VI supports separate voting.
Otherwise the 24 senators are outvoted by more than 300 representatives.
Sitting as a constituent assembly is not sitting as Congress.
src: Art. XVII, Sec. 1(1); V. V. Mendoza; class reviewer; Gatmaytan, ‘Changing Constitutions’

title: Javellana’s votes
ask: How did the ten Justices vote on each question in Javellana v. Executive Secretary (1973)?
items: Justiciable? 6 yes (justiciable), 4 political question.
Validly ratified under Art. XV of the 1935 Constitution? 6 said no.
Accepted by the people? 4 yes; 2 (Concepcion, Zaldivar) no free acceptance under martial law; 4 could not tell.
Relief? 6 voted to dismiss the petitions, 4 to grant.
Result: ‘no further judicial obstacle’ to the 1973 Constitution being considered in force.
src: Javellana v. Executive Secretary (1973)

title: Why the 1973 Constitution was not validly ratified (Concepcion)
ask: Per Concepcion in Javellana, why did the Citizens’ Assemblies not ratify the 1973 Constitution under Art. XV of the 1935 Constitution?
items: Participants were citizens aged 15 and above, not qualified and registered voters.
The questions were not confined to ratification (New Society, martial law reforms, convening Congress).
Voting (e.g., by show of hands) did not follow Art. XV or the Election Code of 1971.
Under martial law, the votes could not show free acceptance; reports were doubtful.
Continued life under the government is not ratification and cures nothing.
src: Javellana (Concepcion, C.J.; Zaldivar, J.)

title: Gatmaytan on Javellana and Lambino
ask: What is Gatmaytan’s reading of Javellana and of Lambino as its counterpoint?
items: Javellana: a majority found no valid ratification, yet the Court ‘looked the other way’.
It removed the judiciary from a position of institutional significance.
It survived martial law but lost public respect; by 1986 seen as subservient to Marcos.
Lambino (2006) was the Court’s redemption: it blocked a government-driven ‘people’s’ initiative despite pressure.
src: Gatmaytan, ‘Changing Constitutions: Judicial Review and Redemption’ (2007)

title: Why Charter change keeps failing (Gatmaytan)
ask: Per Gatmaytan’s ‘Constitutional Amendments as Suspect Projects’, what explains the failure of Charter change?
items: The 1987 Constitution was built as a legal obstacle to dictatorship after Marcos.
Every attempt is seen as a politician’s personal or partisan project to stay in power.
The Supreme Court and civil society have blocked attempts.
Never amended in over 30 years, so protectionist provisions remain.
Changes are doomed unless politicians regain public trust.
src: Gatmaytan, ‘Constitutional Amendments as Suspect Projects’ (2019)

title: Charter change acts the Court will or will not review
ask: Which Charter change acts are reviewable, and which are premature or void, per the cases?
items: Congress acting as a constituent assembly is subject to judicial review (Gonzales).
A decree calling a plebiscite to ratify a constitution is justiciable (Planas).
Whether a constitution was validly ratified is justiciable (Javellana, six Justices).
A House resolution merely calling for a constituent assembly is not ripe (Lozano v. Nograles).
An Executive agreement promising constitutional change is grave abuse (North Cotabato).
src: Gonzales; Planas; Javellana; Lozano; Province of North Cotabato v. GRP

title: Two ways separation of powers is violated
ask: In what two ways is the separation of powers violated (Belgica, per Gatmaytan)?
items: One branch impermissibly interferes with another’s performance of its constitutionally assigned function.
One branch assumes a function that belongs to another.
src: Belgica v. Executive Secretary (2013), cited in Gatmaytan’s book

title: Classic separation-of-powers violations in the materials
ask: Give the four classic separation-of-powers violations in the materials, with their cases.
items: A legislative veto over IRRs by a congressional oversight committee (ABAKADA).
Legislators identifying projects after the budget is enacted (Belgica).
An agency (Tanodbayan) ‘reviewing’ a Supreme Court decision (In re Laureta).
A statute interpreting the Constitution (Endencia).
src: ABAKADA v. Purisima; Belgica; In re Laureta; Endencia

title: When the Court interferes with a co-equal branch
ask: Under Demetria v. Alba, what are the general rule and the exception on judicial interference with another branch?
items: General rule: where a branch acts within the limits of its authority, the Judiciary cannot and ought not interfere.
Exception: where it acts beyond its constitutional authority, the Judiciary must declare the act void.
src: Demetria v. Alba (1987)

title: Angara’s justification and limits of judicial review
ask: Per Angara, why is judicial review not judicial supremacy, and what limits it?
items: Allocating constitutional boundaries asserts no superiority; it is a duty the Constitution assigns.
It is limited to actual cases and controversies.
It is limited further to the constitutional question raised, the lis mota.
Legislative acts enjoy a presumption of constitutionality.
src: Angara v. Electoral Commission (1936)

title: Classical versus expanded judicial review
ask: What distinguishes classical from expanded judicial review?
items: Classical: settle actual controversies involving rights legally demandable and enforceable (Art. VIII, Sec. 1, 2nd para., 1st clause).
Expanded: determine grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction by any branch or instrumentality.
Expanded review was written in response to Martial Law, when the Court hid behind the political question doctrine.
Philippine judicial review is express (Art. VIII, Secs. 1, 4(2), 5(2)); in the US it rests on Marbury v. Madison.
src: Art. VIII, Sec. 1; class reviewer; Gatmaytan

title: Where the Constitution grants judicial review
ask: Which provisions of Art. VIII expressly provide for judicial review, and what do they say?
items: Sec. 1, 2nd para.: judicial power includes settling actual controversies and determining grave abuse of discretion.
Sec. 4(2): constitutionality of a treaty, international or executive agreement, or law is heard en banc.
Sec. 4(2) vote: majority of the Members who actually took part in the deliberations and voted.
Sec. 5(2)(a): SC reviews final judgments where constitutionality or validity of a treaty, law, decree, ordinance or regulation is in question.
Sec. 5(2)(b): SC reviews final judgments on the legality of any tax, impost, assessment or toll, or related penalty.
src: Art. VIII, Secs. 1, 4(2), 5(2)(a)–(b)

title: Functions of judicial review
ask: What are the three functions of judicial review?
items: Checking: invalidating a law or act contrary to the Constitution.
Legitimating: upholding the validity of a law or act.
Symbolic: laying down controlling principles to educate the bench and the bar (basis of a mootness exception).
src: Class reviewer; JR rule map

title: Three levels of scrutiny and their triggers
ask: What are the three levels of scrutiny, and when does each apply?
items: Strict scrutiny: fundamental rights (e.g., travel) or suspect classifications.
Intermediate scrutiny: quasi-suspect classes (sex/gender, illegitimacy) or important but not fundamental rights.
Rational basis: everything else (no suspect class, no fundamental right).
src: Class reviewer (Levels of Scrutiny and the Equal Protection Clause)

title: Elements of strict scrutiny
ask: Under strict scrutiny, what must the government show for the law to stand, and who bears the burden?
items: A compelling State interest (of the highest order).
Means narrowly tailored: the least restrictive means available, no overreach.
Burden on the government (no presumption of validity).
src: Class reviewer; White Light (ordinance failed least-restrictive-means)

title: Elements of intermediate scrutiny
ask: Under intermediate scrutiny, what must the government show?
items: An important governmental objective.
Means substantially related to that objective (strong and logical link).
Need not be the least restrictive means, but must not be overbroad.
src: Class reviewer

title: Elements of rational basis review
ask: Under rational basis review, what is required and who bears the burden?
items: A legitimate government interest (lawful and permissible, not necessarily the highest).
A rational, reasonable connection between the classification and that interest; need not be the best means.
Not arbitrary or irrational.
Law presumed valid; the challenger bears the burden.
src: Class reviewer

title: Two kinds of political questions
ask: A political question is one that, under the Constitution, is to be decided by whom? (two kinds)
items: By the people in their sovereign capacity; or
By the legislative or executive branch, to which full discretionary authority has been delegated.
src: Tañada v. Cuenco definition, in the class reviewer; JR rule map

title: Francisco’s test: truly political or justiciable?
ask: Under Francisco, how do you tell a truly political question from a justiciable one?
items: Ask: does the Constitution impose limits or conditions on the power (vote, time bar, plebiscite, procedure)?
If yes, whether they were observed is justiciable; the Court is duty-bound to decide.
If the matter is wholly left to a political branch with no standard, it is truly political.
Even then, the Court may ask whether there was grave abuse of discretion (Art. VIII, Sec. 1).
src: Francisco v. House (2003)

title: Baker v. Carr formulations (cited in Francisco)
ask: What are the Baker v. Carr indicators of a political question that Francisco cited?
items: A textually demonstrable constitutional commitment of the issue to a coordinate political department.
A lack of judicially discoverable and manageable standards for resolving it.
Impossibility of deciding without an initial policy determination clearly for nonjudicial discretion.
Impossibility of independent resolution without expressing lack of respect due coordinate branches.
An unusual need for unquestioning adherence to a political decision already made.
Potential embarrassment from multifarious pronouncements by various departments on one question.
src: Baker v. Carr, 369 U.S. 186 (1962), as cited in Francisco v. House (2003); not in the class reviewer
hook: Francisco: the first three are the most reliable

title: Justiciable or political? Case examples
ask: Classify these as justiciable or political: the one-year impeachment bar, city conversion plebiscite, constituent assembly acts, project route, urgency certification.
items: Justiciable: the one-year bar on impeachment complaints (Francisco).
Justiciable: the plebiscite needed to convert a city’s status (Miranda v. Aguirre).
Justiciable: Congress acting as constituent assembly (Gonzales).
Political: choosing a project route on grounds of wisdom (Torrecampo).
Political (generally): the factual basis of a presidential urgency certification (Tolentino v. Sec. of Finance).
src: Francisco; Miranda; Gonzales; Torrecampo; Tolentino v. Sec. of Finance

title: Requisites of judicial review
ask: What are the four requisites of judicial review?
items: An actual case or controversy (ripe, not moot).
A proper party with standing (personal and substantial interest; direct injury).
The constitutional question raised at the earliest opportunity.
The constitutional question is the lis mota (necessary to decide the case).
src: Art. VIII, Sec. 1; Angara; Arceta; Lozano

title: Elements of ripeness
ask: When is a question ripe for adjudication? (two elements)
items: The challenged act has been accomplished or performed (reached a final, definitive state).
It has a direct, concrete and adverse effect on the petitioner.
src: Lozano v. Nograles (2009); class reviewer

title: What is not ripe (prematurity cases)
ask: Name the acts held not ripe for judicial review, with their cases.
items: Mere fear that a regulatory power may be abused (PACU).
A bill not yet enacted (Montesclaros; In re JDF).
A House resolution calling for a constituent assembly (Lozano v. Nograles).
Peace agreements that need a law to take effect (PHILCONSA v. Phil. Gov’t, 2016).
The mere passage of a law with no injury to the petitioner (Falcis).
src: PACU; Montesclaros; In re JDF; Lozano; PHILCONSA (2016); Falcis

title: Why a bill cannot be reviewed
ask: Why will the Court not rule on a pending bill?
items: A bill is not a law; it has no legal effect.
It creates no rights and imposes no duties legally demandable and enforceable.
A ruling would be an advisory opinion.
The Court cannot restrain Congress from legislating or review its internal processes (separation of powers).
Judicial review cannot be compelled by mandamus; the remedy is to lobby Congress.
src: Montesclaros v. COMELEC (2002); In re JDF (2015)

title: Exceptions to mootness
ask: What are the four exceptions that let the Court decide a moot case?
items: Grave violation of the Constitution.
Exceptional character of the situation and paramount public interest involved.
Need to formulate controlling principles to guide the bench, the bar and the public.
Capable of repetition yet evading review.
src: David v. Macapagal-Arroyo (2006); Sanlakas (2004); KAPIT (2026)

title: Supervening events that mooted cases
ask: Give the supervening events that mooted cases in the materials.
items: A ruling in another case plus an amendatory law (Atlas Fertilizer).
Lifting of the state-of-rebellion declaration (Lacson v. Perez; Sanlakas, decided anyway as capable of repetition).
Suspension of the ordinances and the 2023 Metro Manila Traffic Code (KAPIT).
Postponement of the plebiscite (Planas).
src: Atlas; Lacson v. Perez; Sanlakas; KAPIT; Planas

title: Grounds for dismissal in KAPIT v. City of Manila
ask: On what grounds were the KAPIT petitions against the no-contact apprehension ordinances dismissed?
items: Moot / no actual case: ordinances suspended and superseded by the 2023 Metro Manila Traffic Code.
No exception to mootness: exceptions apply to the issuance challenged, not an unchallenged successor.
Motorists’ interest alone is not ‘paramount public interest’.
Lack of standing: only one of three petitioners directly affected.
Third-party standing failed: members not identified, nor shown to want the group to sue.
Unregistered associations lacked capacity to sue.
Class reviewer adds: violation of the hierarchy of courts and forum shopping.
src: KAPIT v. City of Manila (2026); class reviewer

title: Direct injury test for standing
ask: What are the elements of the direct injury test for legal standing?
items: Actual or threatened injury from the allegedly illegal government conduct (personal and substantial interest).
Injury fairly traceable to the challenged action.
Injury likely to be redressed by a favorable ruling.
src: AIWA v. Romulo (2005); Joya v. PCGG; IBP v. Zamora

title: Exceptions to the direct injury rule (White Light)
ask: What exceptions to the direct injury requirement does White Light list?
items: Third-party standing.
The overbreadth doctrine.
Taxpayer suits.
Issues of transcendental importance.
src: White Light Corp. v. City of Manila (2009)

title: Kinds of standing and when each is allowed
ask: What are the seven kinds of standing, and when is each allowed?
items: Citizen: enforcing a public right or duty, or transcendental importance (Tañada; Chavez v. PEA).
Taxpayer: illegal disbursement or misuse of public funds, or an unconstitutional tax (ITF).
Voter: obvious interest in the validity of an election law or election (Tolentino 2004).
Legislator: act impairs the prerogatives, powers or privileges of Congress or the legislator (Ople; Sanlakas).
Association/third party: members injured, interest germane; or third-party test (KMU; White Light; GMA).
Government: the State challenging its own law (People v. Vera).
Environment: any Filipino citizen as steward of nature, by citizen suit (Resident Marine Mammals).
src: JR rule map standing table; class reviewer A–G

title: Taxpayer standing denied: no disbursement
ask: Name the cases where taxpayer standing failed because no public funds were disbursed.
items: Joya v. PCGG: auction of property neither theirs nor public; no public funds spent.
AIWA v. Romulo: EO 185 needed no additional appropriation.
Lozano v. Nograles: a House resolution involved no disbursement or allocation of funds.
src: Joya; AIWA; Lozano

title: Requisites and limits of associational standing
ask: When may an association sue for its members, and what are the limits?
items: Its members are injured or stand to be injured (CHREA; KMU).
The interest sought to be protected is germane to the association’s purpose.
It must identify its members and show they want it to sue (KAPIT).
It cannot assert rights of non-members with whom it has no substantial relation (Exec. Sec. v. CA: unskilled workers).
A general interest in the rule of law is not enough (IBP v. Zamora).
An unregistered association lacks capacity to sue (KAPIT).
src: CHREA; KMU; Exec. Sec. v. CA; IBP v. Zamora; KAPIT

title: Requisites of third-party standing
ask: What are the three requisites of third-party standing (White Light)?
items: The litigant suffered an injury-in-fact (sufficiently concrete interest).
The litigant has a close relation to the third party.
Some hindrance prevents the third party from protecting its own interests.
src: White Light Corp. v. City of Manila (2009); applied in GMA Network v. COMELEC

title: Factors of transcendental importance
ask: What three factors determine whether an issue is of transcendental importance?
items: The character of the funds or other assets involved.
A clear case of disregard of a constitutional or statutory prohibition by the respondent.
The lack of any other party with a more direct and specific interest in raising the questions.
src: Francisco v. Fernando / Kilosbayan line, applied in Pangilinan v. Cayetano; IBP v. Zamora (relaxed); AIWA (refused)

title: Gatmaytan’s critique of Pangilinan v. Cayetano
ask: What are Gatmaytan’s objections to the ‘variant technicalities’ in Pangilinan v. Cayetano?
items: Individual legislators’ standing to protect their prerogatives was settled (Biraogo); no Senate act was needed.
Tying standing to an institutional position silences the minority.
A pro-President majority can block any challenge by sitting on a resolution.
Transcendental importance dispenses with standing; ‘better served by actual cases’ is wrong.
Not moot: an invalid withdrawal could not validly take effect.
Even if moot, it fit every exception to mootness.
src: Gatmaytan, ‘Variant Technicalities in Pangilinan v. Cayetano’; class reviewer

title: Gatmaytan on Oposa and environmental standing
ask: What does Gatmaytan argue in ‘The Illusion of Intergenerational Equity’, and how did Resident Marine Mammals change things?
items: Oposa’s pronouncement on standing for future generations was obiter dictum.
It was not needed to resolve the real issue: whether petitioners had a cause of action.
The present/future distinction is inconsequential: protect the present to protect the future.
Future generations are already recognized in law and in the framers’ intent for Art. II, Sec. 16.
Resident Marine Mammals: no need to give animals personality; any citizen may file a citizen suit (RPEC).
src: Gatmaytan, ‘The Illusion of Intergenerational Equity’ (2003); Oposa v. Factoran; Resident Marine Mammals (2015)

title: Rules on earliest opportunity
ask: What does the ‘earliest opportunity’ requisite mean, and what are its qualifications?
items: Raise the constitutional issue at the first chance, in the pleadings before a competent court.
It cannot be raised for the first time on appeal, unless that court has original jurisdiction.
The Supreme Court may, in its discretion, take up a constitutional issue raised later.
It does not mean suing as soon as a law passes; a regulation may be challenged when enforced (Gatmaytan).
src: Arceta v. Mangrobang (2004); class reviewer; Gatmaytan’s book

title: Lis mota: what it requires
ask: What does the lis mota requisite require?
items: The case cannot be resolved without deciding the constitutional question.
If it can be decided on another ground, the Court uses that ground.
The petitioner bears the burden of showing the question is unavoidable.
Rests on the presumption of constitutionality; doubts are resolved for validity.
src: Arceta v. Mangrobang (2004); Angara; class reviewer

title: Why Falcis was dismissed
ask: On what procedural grounds was Falcis v. Civil Registrar General dismissed?
items: No actual case: the mere passage of the Family Code created none.
No standing: he never applied for a marriage license (no injury).
Wrong respondent and wrong relief.
Violation of the hierarchy of courts.
Not raised at the earliest opportunity (Family Code in force since 1988, per the class reviewer).
src: Falcis III v. Civil Registrar General (2019); class reviewer (Gatmaytan ‘really doesn’t like this decision’)

title: Why Arceta was dismissed
ask: Why were the petitions in Arceta v. Mangrobang (challenging BP 22) dismissed?
items: Not raised at the earliest opportunity: no motion to quash in the trial court.
Not the lis mota: no constitutional issue was raised or argued below.
Violation of the hierarchy of courts (went straight to the Supreme Court).
No allegation of grave abuse against the respondent judges for certiorari.
src: Arceta v. Mangrobang (2004)

title: Orthodox effects of an unconstitutional law
ask: Under the orthodox view (Civil Code, Art. 7), what are the effects of an unconstitutional act?
items: It confers no rights.
It imposes no duties.
It affords no protection.
It creates no office.
It is inoperative, as if it had never been passed.
src: Civil Code, Art. 7; Norton v. Shelby County (orthodox view)

title: Operative fact doctrine: rule and applications
ask: State the operative fact doctrine and its applications and limits in the materials.
items: Rule: good-faith acts done in reliance on the law before its nullification may be respected, to avoid injustice.
Araullo: applied to DAP projects that could not be undone.
Araullo: not to authors and implementors absent findings of good faith.
Macalintal (2023): the October 2023 barangay elections proceeded.
Refused where it would reward the beneficiary of the void law (Planters Products v. Fertiphil).
src: Araullo v. Aquino (2014); Macalintal v. COMELEC (2023); Planters Products v. Fertiphil

title: Partial unconstitutionality and separability
ask: When does the valid part of a partly unconstitutional law survive, and what is Gatmaytan’s view?
items: The valid part stands if separable from the void part.
It falls if the parts are so dependent that Congress meant them as a whole.
It falls if what remains is incomplete and cannot be carried out as intended.
A separability clause creates only a presumption of separability.
Gatmaytan: severability should not depend on a clause (usual approach; the US rule).
src: JR rule map; Gatmaytan’s book

title: Remedies and forum quick guide
ask: Match the dispute to the proper remedy or forum.
items: Grave abuse by a branch: certiorari or prohibition under Rule 65 (direct to the SC only for transcendental issues).
A law not yet violated: declaratory relief in the RTC (Exec. Sec. v. CA; White Light).
Election dispute before the winner becomes a Member: COMELEC.
After proclamation, oath and assumption: HRET or SET.
President or Vice President: the Supreme Court as PET.
Money claims against the State: COA first (Fetalvero).
src: JR rule map (Remedies and forum); Art. VI, Sec. 17; Art. VII, Sec. 4
